newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Cathay sees 100 aircraft fleet in 5 years.
newsitem.headline: Cathay sees 100 aircraft fleet in 5 years.

text.p: Cathay Pacific Airways Ltd chairman Peter Sutch said he expected to have more than 100 aircraft within five years compared to the present 59.

The carrier also expects to fly to 10 or more new destinations, he said in an interview with Orient Aviation, the magazine of the 18 member Association of Asia-Pacific Airlines (formerly the Orient Airlines Association).

Sutch added he is confident about Cathay's future after the handover of Hong Kong at the end of the month. Looking back over the past 13 years since the signing of the Joint Declaration, he said the transition had gone more smoothly than one could have expected.

He added that last year's share restructuring confirmed his belief in the future. This saw China-backed CITIC Pacific Ltd take a 25 per cent stake in Cathay while China National Aviation Corp and bought a 36 per cent controlling stake in Hong Kong Dragon Airlines.
Sutch said he thought it will be another three to six months before the financial community realises that Swire Pacific Ltd and Cathay Pacific stock is sound "and indeed has a bright future."
The chairman said Cathay will face more competition from Chinese carriers after the opening of Hong Kong's new Chek Lap Kok airport in 1998," but competition is not new to us."
"Business between Hong Kong and China in the future will require some give and take on both sides," Sutch said.

It is also possible Cathay will have a local managing director, he said. The recently appointed current deputy is Philip Chen and industry sources suggest he is as being groomed to take control from the current managing director, David Turnbull.
Sutch also did not rule out closer links with Chinese and other international carriers.

"We want to become a real part of the Greater China aviation community and while our policy on alliances has been somewhat cautious in the past it is possible we will forge new links with Chinese and/or other airlines.
"This is likely to take the form of straight but close commercial arrangements held together by mutual benefit for the participants and their customers, rather than by equity," Sutch said.
